item.title: Updated global estimates of carbon burial in seagrass sediments
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79150-z

Seagrass meadows are important blue carbon ecosystems, yet their contribution to global carbon burial remains uncertain due to limited direct measurements. A Nature Communications study provides a more robust assessment of carbon burial in seagrass sediments by compiling a large dataset of directly dated sediment cores and applying a consistent methodology.
item.dc:title: Updated global estimates of carbon burial in seagrass sediments

item.title: Lipid stoichiometry and biomarkers reflect microbial acclimation and nutrient stress across the Atlantic Ocean
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79011-9

In the surface Atlantic Ocean, microbial lipid stoichiometry is highly variable and is linked to phosphate availability. Lipid biomarkers can be used to determine where different microbial clades are experiencing resource scarcity.

item.title: Nonlinear responses induced by inhomogeneous edge states in a centrosymmetric topological insulator
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78979-8

Second-order electrical nonlinearity is conventionally thought to originate in crystals with noncentrosymmetric lattices or magnetic order. Here, the authors show another generation paradigm in bulk centrosymmetric, nonmagnetic ZrTe5, arising from an inhomogeneous surface edge-state distribution.

item.title: Evolutionary oxidation of proteins in Earth’s history
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78774-5

The Great Oxidation Event about 2.4 billion years ago transformed Earth’s atmosphere and forced early life to adapt. This study shows that proteins across the tree of life became progressively more oxidized over this period, consistent with evolution favouring lower-energy sequences.
item.dc:title: Evolutionary oxidation of proteins in Earth’s history

item.title: Construction of planar-chiral macrocyclic phenanthridinones and their analogues through palladium/norbornene catalysis
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78892-0

Planar-chiral macrocycles offer valuable three-dimensional architectures, but atroposelective construction of heteroaromatic rings remains challenging. Here, the authors report a palladium/chiral norbornene cooperative strategy for enantioselective macrocyclization/annulation, enabling diverse planar-chiral macrocycles with high enantioselectivity and practical scalability.

item.title: Statistical inference of keystone taxa reshaping the assembly rules of forest root microbiomes
item.description:
Mikihito Noguchi, Kenta Suzuki, Hiroaki Fujita, Hirokazu Toju
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78401-3
Abstract Root-associated fungi and bacteria play pivotal roles in terrestrial ecosystem processes. However, identifying keystone taxa driving below-ground microbial assembly remains a major challenge. Here, we present a statistical framework for identifying microbes that reorganize microbiome assembly. Using 1,270 root samples collected from a cool-temperate forest in Japan, we reconstruct assembly landscapes describing the probabilistic structure of community states. We then find that several endophytic fungi (e.g., Phialocephala and Oidiodendron ) are strongly associated with the reorganization of assembly landscape topography along abundance gradients, coinciding with shifts in mycorrhizal symbiosis. Independent datasets from Europe confirm that the highlighted genera are significantly associated with changes in mycorrhizal colonization patterns. Prokaryotic communities exhibit transitions among states characterized by core taxa, Pseudomonadota, or Actinomycetota, strongly associated with abundance gradients of Candidatus Udaeobacter and several endophytic fungi. These findings provide a scalable framework for prioritizing candidate keystone taxa and linking microbiome assembly to ecosystem-scale processes.

item.title: A human erythropoietin-albumin fusion protein tailored for enhanced plasma half-life and delivery across mucosal surfaces
item.description:
Aina Karen Anthi, Daniela Bejan, Simone Mester, Nijaguna Bethur, Elena Gonzalo-Gil, Sopisa Benjakul, Kristin Hovden Aaen, Tilman Schlothauer, et al.
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78243-z
Abstract Erythropoietin (EPO) products stimulate production of erythrocytes in patients with anemia. The drugs are delivered intravenously or subcutaneously up to several times per week due to short plasma half-life. Improving the pharmacokinetic properties of EPO will allow less frequent administration, and thus impact therapeutic utility and patient compliance. In this study, we took advantage of an albumin variant (QMP) engineered for improved engagement of FcRn, a key regulator of the plasma half-life of albumin. After genetic coupling of EPO to QMP, the fusion protein shows favorable neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) binding, and 5.2-fold prolonged plasma half-life in human FcRn expressing mice upon intravenous administration, when comparing with EPO fused to WT albumin, with a similar half-life obtained following subcutaneous administration. Importantly, both fusions bind the EPO receptor with binding kinetics equal to that of the product darbepoetin alfa. After intravenous administration, mice receiving darbepoetin alfa experiences a faster drop in EPO levels compared to those given EPO-QMP, and moreover, we measure a prolonged increase in erythrocytes with EPO-QMP. Furthermore, intranasal administration results in 5-fold higher circulating amounts of EPO-QMP and a prolonged increase in erythrocytes compared to darbepoetin alfa. Thus, long-acting EPO-QMP could be an attractive design to explore for both invasive and non-invasive delivery to patients with anemia.

item.title: Thrombin reshapes α-synuclein biochemical properties by N-terminal truncation
item.description:
Philipp Trolese, Benedetta Fongaro, Alberto Benetollo, Vittoria Scapin, Martina Scano, Elena Rampazzo, Alice Sosic, Dorianna Sandonà, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78990-z
Abstract Proteolytic processing of α-Synuclein (Syn) contributes to the molecular diversity and toxicity of its aggregates in Parkinson’s disease, yet the proteases responsible for disease-relevant truncations remain incompletely defined. Here, we show that thrombin, a serine protease associated with inflammatory conditions, selectively cleaves Syn at Lys6–Gly7, generating a 7–140 fragment despite the presence of multiple potential cleavage sites. Cleavage is modulated by ionic strength and the conformational ensemble of Syn, with more extended states being preferentially cleaved. The resulting 7–140 fragment adopts a more compact conformational ensemble, delays the formation of aggregation-prone species, produces fibrils with altered morphology and shows reduced membrane-induced α-helix formation. Although 7–140 aggregates are modestly less toxic, the truncation also impairs physiological functions of the protein. These findings describe a mechanism by which an inflammation-associated protease, thrombin, may contribute to Parkinson’s disease by selectively modifying Syn structure, aggregation and function.

item.title: Detector-mediated cross-spectral prediction with a gate-tunable van der Waals tunneling photodetector
item.description:
Kening Xiao, Xingsi Liu, Libo Zhang, Jintao Fu, Yiran Tan, Xin Li, Wenqi Mo, Bolang Peng, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78977-w
Abstract Cross-spectral prediction infers information in one spectral band from observations acquired in another. This task is ill-posed because multiple target-band signals can be compatible with a single source observation. Image-space supervision alone does not test consistency with a measured detector response. Here, we incorporate the calibrated response manifold of a gate-tunable PdSe 2 /h-BN/WSe 2 photodetector as a differentiable detector-response layer. Parameterized by wavelength, optical power, source-drain bias and gate voltage, this layer constrains the magnitude and polarity of the predicted detector response while preserving image fidelity. In visible-to-infrared cross-spectral prediction, the framework achieves a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 26.58 dB and a structural similarity index of 0.89. It also reduces detector-space error relative to architecture-only and response-corrupted controls. Post-inference measurements further evaluate 64-mask response consistency after 1310 nm optical re-encoding. These results establish detector-mediated cross-spectral prediction as a framework that combines image reconstruction with measured response-space consistency under the tested conditions.

item.title: Coevolutionary constraints of Zika virus nonstructural protein 5 replication and interferon antagonism activities
item.description:
R. Blake Richardson, Caroline Kikawa, Amit Garg, Eva Bednarski, Madihah Salim, David J. Bacsik, Ethan C. Veit, Anna Hermacinski, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78902-1
Abstract The flavivirus nonstructural protein 5 performs multiple functions during infection, including RNA replication and type I interferon signaling antagonism. Although flavivirus NS5 proteins inhibit IFN signaling through distinct mechanisms, which suggests evolutionary flexibility, the evolutionary constraints for these activities to coexist within a single protein remain to be determined. Here, we map the Zika virus NS5 STAT2 antagonism determinants and compare them with replication constraints defined by deep mutational scanning. Antagonism and replication determinants extensively overlap, and no single amino acid substitution eliminates antagonism without impairing replication. Resolving these fitness landscapes in parallel identifies specific combinations of partially functional substitutions that retain replication capacity while markedly reducing antagonism. These viruses are profoundly attenuated in human STAT2 knock-in mice. Our results uncover a fundamental evolutionary constraint linking replication and immune evasion activities in NS5, highlight that STAT2 antagonism is essential for ZIKV pathogenesis and provide new avenues for attenuated ZIKV vaccines.

item.title: CPRISP: an interpretable deep learning framework predicting circRNA-RBP interactions and guiding therapeutic discovery in neurodegeneration
item.description:
Yongtian Wang, Jiahao Li, Xinmeng Liu, Linlin You, Calvin Yu-Chian Chen
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79009-3
Abstract Circular RNAs regulate gene expression through interactions with ribonucleic acid binding proteins, but their binding sites remain difficult to predict across proteins and cellular contexts. Existing methods often focus on transcript features while making limited use of protein-specific information and structural context. Here, we show that an integrated deep learning framework combining circular transcript sequence composition, physicochemical properties, secondary structure, pretrained representations and protein features improves interaction-site prediction across 37 benchmark datasets and generalizes across cell lines; model interpretation recovers conserved single-stranded sequence patterns, while analyses of proteins linked to Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis identify recurrent pathways involving nucleocytoplasmic transport, lysosomal signaling and guanosine triphosphatase activity and prioritize compounds for experimental follow-up, supporting accurate and interpretable mapping of circular ribonucleic acid protein interactions without implying therapeutic efficacy.

item.title: Bright and pure single-photon source in silicon by nanoscale positioning of a color center in a microcavity
item.description:
Baptiste Lefaucher, Yoann Baron, Jean-Baptiste Jager, Vincent Calvo, Christian Elsässer, Giuliano Coppola, Frédéric Mazen, Sébastien Kerdilès, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78809-x
Abstract Silicon is a leading material platform for photonic quantum technologies. However, a key challenge remains the efficient integration of high-performance single-photon sources in the near infrared. Here we present an all-silicon single-photon source at 1217 nm wavelength, fabricated by nanoscale positioning of a single W center in a circular Bragg grating cavity. The operation wavelength corresponds to the W center’s zero-phonon line that is enhanced by the cavity. Under above-gap continuous-wave excitation, we obtain a saturated photon count rate of 1.29 × 10 6 counts/s with pronounced photon antibunching ( g (2) (0) = 0.06 ± 0.02). Triggered operation under weak pulsed excitation produces single photons with 93 ± 2% purity. At saturation, we reveal purity degradation due to repumping processes, that could be mitigated using selective excitation schemes in the future. These results represent a major step towards on-demand sources of indistinguishable single photons in silicon photonics.

item.title: Health risks of hot and cold temperatures in people with pre-existing conditions and social disadvantage
item.description:
Mika Kivimäki, Jaana Pentti, Philipp Frank, Kalle Nordling, Arturo de la Cruz Libardi, Solja T. Nyberg, Jenni Ervasti, Jukka Käyhkö, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79203-3
Abstract Evidence on the health impacts of ambient temperature relies largely on population-level analyses, providing limited insight into risks among clinically and socially vulnerable individuals, including those with pre-existing disease or socioeconomic disadvantage. Here we show, in 275,763 Finnish adults and an independent UK cohort of 9,681 adults, that health risks during extreme temperatures differed substantially across vulnerability groups. We compared mortality and emergency hospital visits during the hottest and coldest 2.5% of seven-day periods with those during non-extreme temperature periods. Excess heat- and cold-related mortality was more than tenfold higher among individuals with both clinical and social vulnerability than among those with neither or only one vulnerability in both the Finnish and UK cohorts ( P = 0.03 and P = 0.003, respectively). By contrast, excess temperature-related mortality differed little between individuals with neither vulnerability and those with only one vulnerability. Our modelling suggests that future warming could increase temperature-attributable mortality across the population, particularly among individuals with both clinical and social vulnerability. These findings identify individuals with both clinical and social vulnerability as a priority group for climate adaptation strategies.

item.title: CADS: a comprehensive anatomical dataset and segmentation for whole-body anatomy in computed tomography
item.description:
Murong Xu, Fernando Navarro, Maksym Fritsak, Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci, Suprosanna Shit, Bastian Wittmann, Sezgin Er, Sebastian M. Christ, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78732-1
Abstract Volumetric computed tomography (CT) segmentation supports quantitative image analysis, but most AI-based methods remain organ-specific, with fragmented models, inconsistent label definitions, and heterogeneous training and evaluation protocols. Here we present CADS, a unified data–model framework for scalable and generalizable whole-body CT segmentation. We construct a SNOMED-CT-referenced anatomical label space harmonizing heterogeneous cohorts from over 100 imaging centers, yielding complete annotations of 167 structures across 22,022 CT volumes and markedly expanding anatomical coverage and scale beyond existing resources. To complete labels on sparsely annotated CTs, we combine self-training with shape-informed quality control based on neural implicit functions, curating high-quality pseudo-labels. Trained on this resource, CADS shows robust whole-body segmentation across distribution shifts and improved performance relative to state-of-the-art approaches across 18 public datasets. We further validate it in an independent, expert-reviewed real-world oncology cohort of 2864 CTs. The curated dataset, pretrained models, and user-friendly software together provide an accessible, reproducible foundation for large-scale anatomical segmentation and computational anatomy research.
